claims.text: Sustained high-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by the ability to form a coherent and adherent alumina-based protective scale.
Changing aluminum content while holding the other alloying components constant changes the alloy's ability to form a protective alumina scale.
A coherent, dense, and adherent alumina-based surface scale is the structural mediator of oxidation resistance.
At high temperatures, aluminum diffuses through the alloy toward the surface.
Surface-arriving aluminum oxidizes to form a protective alumina scale.
Sufficient aluminum content produces a stable, passivating oxide layer.
High mixing entropy in a multiprincipal-element alloy limits diffusion.
High mixing entropy promotes a uniform oxide-scale structure.
Higher-aluminum alloy variants will form a more stable and adherent alumina scale than lower-aluminum variants.
Higher-aluminum alloy variants will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics, represented by lower net mass gain.
Higher-aluminum alloy variants will retain mechanical integrity better than lower-aluminum variants after oxidation.
A lower-aluminum baseline will form a less effective oxide scale.
A less effective oxide scale in the lower-aluminum baseline will cause higher oxidation rates and reduced mechanical integrity.
The proposed behavior holds in the temperature range where alumina formation is favored and after exposures long enough for the scale to approach steady state.
At temperatures too low for adequate scale formation, the proposed behavior may not apply.
At excessively high temperatures, loss of scale stability may invalidate the proposed behavior.
